name: Aspirin
summary: A unique NSAID because irreversible platelet COX-1 inhibition gives it a lasting antiplatelet effect at low doses.
good: Secondary prevention in the right cardiovascular context and select acute coronary scenarios.
bad: Anyone with substantial bleeding risk or an active peptic ulcer problem.
clinicalPearls: Low-dose aspirin is a platelet drug first and a pain drug second.
mechanism: Irreversible acetylation of COX-1 and COX-2; in platelets, COX-1 blockade reduces thromboxane A2 for the life of the platelet.
indications: Secondary prevention of atherosclerotic events, acute coronary syndromes, and analgesic/antipyretic use at higher doses.
interactionNotes: Other antiplatelets, anticoagulants, SSRIs, and ibuprofen timing can all matter.

warnings: Bleeding, active ulcer disease, late pregnancy, and pediatric viral illness are classic avoid/strong-caution settings.

originalFields: Mechanism
Irreversible acetylation of COX-1 and COX-2; in platelets, COX-1 blockade reduces thromboxane A2 for the life of the platelet.
Typical uses
Secondary prevention of atherosclerotic events, acute coronary syndromes, and analgesic/antipyretic use at higher doses.
Key cautions
Bleeding, active ulcer disease, late pregnancy, and pediatric viral illness are classic avoid/strong-caution settings.
Important interactions
Other antiplatelets, anticoagulants, SSRIs, and ibuprofen timing can all matter.
Pearl
Low-dose aspirin is a platelet drug first and a pain drug second.
COX selectivity
Nonselective, but the irreversible platelet effect at low dose is what defines its clinical identity.
GI risk
Elevated even at cardioprotective (75–100mg) doses, because platelet COX-1 inhibition is essentially complete at low dose.
CV / antiplatelet effect
The one NSAID with a genuine antiplatelet benefit — irreversible thromboxane A₂ suppression reduces clot formation.
Renal risk
Present at anti-inflammatory doses; minimal at low antiplatelet doses.
Typical use here
Low-dose: cardiovascular/stroke prophylaxis. High-dose: analgesic/anti-inflammatory use is now uncommon given safer alternatives.
